Now the big architecture: clauses inside clauses. I know that... The woman who... When the boat comes... If you do that... In Gupapuyŋu, an enormous amount of this is carried by one word: ŋunhi.

ŋunhi = that (reporting):
Ŋarra ŋäkula ŋunhi gäthura walala waṉḏina → I heard that they ran away today
Ŋarra marŋgi ŋunhi nhe ŋuli djäma bitjan bili → I know that you work every day

(Look at that second one paying off three lessons at once: marŋgi, ŋuli, bitjan bili.)

And, very often, you can drop the ŋunhi entirely and just butt the clauses together:
Nhe marŋgi ŋarraku bäpa dhiŋgaŋala dhiyala → You know my father died here. Clauses side by side, no glue, totally natural.

ŋunhi = who/which (relative clauses):
Ŋarra dhägir'yurruna djamarrkuḻi'nha ŋunhi barpuru walala ŋatha manaŋirri → I punished the children who stole the food yesterday

Notice the walala tucked in after ŋunhi, literally: the children, that THEY stole the food. Gupapuyŋu keeps a pronoun in the relative clause where English leaves a gap. The who is really that + they. Once you see it, relative clauses stop being scary: they're just a pointed that with a pronoun echo.

ŋunhi / ŋuli / bäy = when:
Ŋunhi mitjiyaŋ dhu marrtji ŋarra dhu gurrupan nhokala → When the boat comes, I'll give it to you

Three interchangeable openers: ŋunhi, ŋuli, bäy. And catch the tense! The boat WILL come, dhu, right there in the when-clause. English says when the boat comes (present); Gupapuyŋu says the honest thing: it hasn't come yet, so it's future. When the boat will come. The grammar refuses to pretend the future already happened.

ŋuli / ŋunhi / balaŋu = if:
Ŋuli mitjiyaŋ dhu marrtji ŋarra dhu gurrupan nhokala → IF the boat comes, I'll give it to you

Yes, the same little words, now doing if. When and if blur into each other here, and honestly, that's philosophically fair: every when about the future carries a quiet if inside it. You can stack them for emphasis (ŋuli balaŋu...), and slip a ga before the main clause to hinge the two halves.

One word, ŋunhi, holding up reporting, relatives, time and condition. Keep it in your pocket. Next lesson: the rest of the family, because, until, before, after, whether.
